I’ve been farming these 6 mu in Quzhou for 30 years, and I know this soil like the back of my hand. My father taught me, and I’ve watched the wheat-maize rotation year after year. With four mouths to feed and a well I can rely on, I stick to what works: wheat in the winter, maize in the summer, every inch of the 6 mu working twice a year.

For the wheat, I’ll sow in early October when the autumn rain softens the ground. I always rotary-till before planting—loosens the soil and buries the maize stubble. I buy improved wheat seed from the village supply shop; the old traditional varieties don’t resist disease anymore. I put down about 100 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing, and I top-dress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. Water is life here, so I irrigate three times from the well: once before winter to help it survive the cold, once at jointing, and once at heading. I spray pesticides two or three times when I see aphids or rust starting. If the weather treats me fair, I expect around 1,000 jin of wheat per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I plant maize the same day—no time to waste. I use hybrid seed, always hybrid; the yield is too good to pass up. I don’t till for maize; I drill the seed straight into the wheat stubble. One bag of compound fertilizer per mu goes down at planting, and I might throw on a bit of urea at the big-trumpet stage if the leaves look pale. I irrigate twice from the well—once when it’s young and once when the tassels come out. I spray for insects and weeds two or three times over the summer. A good summer should give me about 1,200 jin of maize per mu.

This is the way I’ve always done it, and it keeps my family fed and the grain dealer coming back.
